title: 22. Interview: Data Lake
summary: Interview Q&A for Data Lake — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Data Lake interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What is the difference between schema-on-write and schema-on-read, and why does the data lake prefer the latter?
**Answer:** Schema-on-write (the warehouse model) enforces a schema at ingestion time: each record is parsed, validated, type-cast, and rejected if it does not fit the predefined table schema, before being stored. The benefit is data quality and query performance (typed columns, partition pruning, columnar compression); the cost is rigidity — new fields, new sources, and new event types require schema migrations that can take days to coordinate. Schema-on-read (the lake model) stores raw bytes without enforcing a schema, and applies the schema only when a query reads the data — the analyst declares "treat column X as int" at query time, and the engine parses on the fly. The benefit is flexibility: new sources land in minutes without coordination, and analysts can explore raw data before deciding on a model. The cost is query performance (parsing JSON per query is slower than reading typed Parquet) and data quality (junk data accumulates). The lake prefers schema-on-read because its central value proposition is "store everything now, ask questions later" — you cannot always predict the schema at ingestion, especially for clickstreams with evolving event types or partner data with unfamiliar formats. The modern lakehouse (Delta/Iceberg) bridges the two: raw zone is schema-on-read, curated zone is schema-on-write.
**Visual:**
```
schema-on-write (warehouse): parse+validate+cast at ingest -> reject bad rows
schema-on-read (lake):       store raw bytes -> parse at query time
lakehouse:                   raw zone = schema-on-read, curated = schema-on-write
```

### Q2. What are the data lake zones, and why are they separated?
**Answer:** The canonical zone model has three layers: raw (bronze), curated (silver), and consumption (gold). The **raw zone** preserves data exactly as it arrived from source — no transformation, no schema enforcement — partitioned by source and ingestion date; it serves as the immutable system of record for replay and audit. The **curated zone** holds cleaned, deduplicated, type-cast data in an open columnar format (Parquet) with a defined schema registered in the metastore; it serves as the conformance layer where data quality is enforced. The **consumption zone** holds business-level aggregates, feature stores, and materialized views designed for specific use cases (BI dashboards, ML training, regulatory reports). Separating zones enforces a one-way data flow: raw → curated → consumption, with each transition applying transformations and quality checks. This separation provides three benefits: (1) replayability — if a transformation bug is found in curated, you can rebuild from raw; (2) isolation — a schema change in raw does not break consumers until curated is rebuilt; (3) access control — raw can be restricted to data engineers, curated open to analysts, consumption open to business users. Without zones, the lake becomes a swamp where every consumer reads from raw and re-implements parsing independently.
**Visual:**
```
raw (bronze):   immutable, no schema, partitioned by dt/source
curated (silver): cleaned, typed Parquet, schema in metastore
gold:           business aggregates, feature stores, dashboards
flow:           raw --> (ETL) --> curated --> (dbt) --> gold
```

### Q3. What is the "data swamp" anti-pattern, and how do you avoid it?
**Answer:** A data swamp is a data lake that has grown without governance: thousands of datasets, undocumented schemas, unknown owners, duplicative tables, broken pipelines, and no way for an analyst to find trustworthy data. Symptoms include analysts spending 80% of their time hunting for data and verifying its quality, duplicate tables with conflicting numbers, and pipelines failing silently. The causes are operational, not technical: no catalog (analysts cannot discover datasets), no lineage (cannot trace a metric to its source), no schema enforcement (raw junk propagates to curated), no ownership (orphaned tables nobody maintains), and no access control (anyone can write anywhere). To avoid it, treat the lake as a product: (1) implement a catalog (AWS Glue, DataHub, Amundsen) with discovery, schema, and ownership metadata; (2) enforce lineage tracking (OpenLineage, Spline) so every dataset shows its upstream sources; (3) require schema registration at the curated zone boundary, rejecting untyped data; (4) assign every dataset an owner (team, on-call rotation) and a freshness SLA; (5) implement access controls (Apache Ranger, Lake Formation) with audit logging; (6) run automated quality checks (Great Expectations, dbt tests) that fail pipelines on bad data. The discipline is ongoing — without active gardening, any lake becomes a swamp within 2–3 years.
**Visual:**
```
data lake (healthy):  catalog + lineage + ownership + schema + quality checks
data swamp (decayed): no catalog, no lineage, orphan tables, raw junk in curated
fix:                  treat lake as product, automate governance, audit access
```

### Q4. What is a lakehouse, and how does it differ from a data lake?
**Answer:** A lakehouse is a data lake augmented with warehouse-like transactional semantics, combining the cheap open storage of the lake with the ACID, schema enforcement, and time travel of the warehouse. The three open table formats enabling this are Delta Lake (Databricks), Apache Iceberg (Netflix, now widely adopted), and Apache Hudi (Uber). Each provides ACID transactions on top of Parquet files in object storage by maintaining a metadata log (Delta: JSON transaction log; Iceberg: Avro manifest list; Hudi: timeline) that tracks which files belong to which snapshot. A lakehouse table supports concurrent writers with optimistic concurrency, schema evolution (add/rename columns without rewriting), time travel (query the table as of a past timestamp), upserts and deletes (not just appends), and schema enforcement (reject rows that don't match). The differences from a pure lake: (1) pure lakes have no transactions — concurrent writers can corrupt each other; (2) pure lakes have no time travel — once overwritten, the old data is gone; (3) pure lakes have no schema enforcement — junk data accumulates. The lakehouse adds these without sacrificing the lake's flexibility (open Parquet, cheap S3, ML-friendly). It does add operational complexity (managing the table format, compaction, manifest maintenance) and is slower than a native warehouse for high-throughput updates.
**Visual:**
```
pure lake:     S3 + Parquet, no transactions, no time travel, no schema enforcement
lakehouse:     S3 + Parquet + Delta/Iceberg/Hudi metadata log
benefits:      ACID, schema enforcement, time travel, upserts
trade-off:     metadata log management, compaction, slightly slower updates
```

### Q5. How do Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg, and Apache Hudi differ?
**Answer:** All three are open table formats that bring ACID to data lakes, but they differ in origin, design, and strengths. **Delta Lake** (Databricks, 2017) stores a JSON transaction log (`_delta_log/`) listing all operations; it integrates tightly with Spark, supports time travel and upserts via MERGE, and is the simplest to adopt if you're already on Databricks. **Apache Iceberg** (Netflix, 2018) uses an Avro manifest list and a hierarchical metadata tree that scales to petabytes without performance degradation; its key innovation is hidden partitioning (partition by `event_date` derived from `event_timestamp`, transparent to the query) and fast planning (manifests avoid listing S3 files). Iceberg has the broadest engine support (Spark, Trino, Flink, Snowflake, BigQuery). **Apache Hudi** (Uber, 2017) was built for incremental upserts on CDC streams — its strength is near-real-time ingestion with primary-key-based upserts and incremental queries (read "all changes since time T"). Hudi supports both Copy-on-Write (slower writes, fast reads) and Merge-on-Read (fast writes, slower reads). Choose Iceberg for analytical workloads with broad engine support, Delta for Databricks-centric platforms, Hudi for streaming-heavy upsert workloads. All three are converging in features, so the choice increasingly comes down to ecosystem fit.
**Visual:**
```
Delta (Databricks): JSON tx log, Spark-native, simplest in Databricks
Iceberg (Netflix):  Avro manifest tree, hidden partitioning, broadest engine support
Hudi (Uber):        timeline, PK upserts, incremental queries, streaming-first
```

### Q6. Why partition data lake tables by date, and what are the pitfalls?
**Answer:** Date partitioning (e.g., `dt=2024-03-15/`) is the foundational optimization for data lake queries: most analytical queries filter by date ("show me yesterday's revenue"), and partition pruning lets the engine skip entire directories without reading their files. Without partitioning, a query for one day's data would scan the entire table (potentially petabytes); with partitioning, it scans one day's worth (a few GB). The pitfalls are: (1) **over-partitioning** — partitioning by hour or by a high-cardinality column (like `user_id`) creates millions of tiny directories, each with a small file; the metastore bloats, S3 LIST operations slow, and the small-files problem kills query performance. Rule of thumb: each partition should have at least 1GB of data. (2) **under-partitioning** — not partitioning at all means every query scans the full table, defeating the purpose. (3) **wrong partition column** — partitioning by a column that's rarely filtered on (like `region` when most queries are time-based) provides no benefit. (4) **partition skew** — if 80% of events are on a single day (e.g., a Black Friday spike), that partition is much larger and slower than others. The right approach: partition by date (day for most workloads, hour only for very high-volume streams), maybe add a second low-cardinality column (like `region` or `event_type`) if queries filter on it, and use Iceberg's hidden partitioning so analysts don't need to remember the partition column.
**Visual:**
```
good:   dt=2024-03-15/  (1-10GB per partition, easy pruning)
bad:    dt=2024-03-15/00/01/02/...  (tiny files, small-files problem)
bad:    user_id=u1234/  (millions of partitions, metastore bloat)
rule:   each partition >= 1GB, cardinality < 10K partitions per table
```

### Q7. How do you handle PII (personally identifiable information) in a data lake?
**Answer:** PII handling in a data lake requires defense in depth because the lake stores raw, immutable data — once PII lands in the raw zone, removing it is hard. The standard approach: (1) **tokenize at ingestion** — replace PII fields (email, SSN, phone) with deterministic tokens before writing to the raw zone, using a vault service that maps tokens to original values with strict access control. (2) **encrypt at rest** — S3 server-side encryption (SSE-KMS) with customer-managed KMS keys, so even physical disk theft cannot expose PII. (3) **column-level access control** — use Apache Ranger or Lake Formation to grant column-level privileges, so a junior analyst can see `user_id` but not `email` or `phone`. (4) **dynamic data masking** — Trino and Spark support views that mask PII on read (e.g., `email -> 'j***@example.com'`) for analysts without full access. (5) **audit logging** — log every access to PII columns for compliance (GDPR, CCPA, HIPAA). (6) **data retention policies** — lifecycle rules that delete or anonymize PII after a retention period (e.g., 90 days for raw clickstream). (7) **GDPR right-to-erasure** — for Iceberg/Delta tables, use the row-level DELETE to remove a specific user's records and rewrite the affected files. The hardest case is PII in free-text fields (chat transcripts, support tickets) — those require NLP-based PII detection (AWS Comprehend, Presidio) to redact before storage.
**Visual:**
```
ingest: tokenize PII -> raw zone has tokens, not real PII
at rest: S3 SSE-KMS encryption with customer-managed keys
access: column-level (Ranger/Lake Formation), dynamic masking in views
audit:  log every read of PII columns -> compliance dashboard
retire: lifecycle delete after 90d, Iceberg row DELETE for erasure
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. You are building a clickstream analytics platform for an e-commerce site with 10M daily active users generating 5B events/day. Design the data lake.
**Answer:** Architecture: Kafka ingest (5B events/day = ~60K events/sec peak) → S3 raw zone via Kinesis Firehose (1-minute rotation, 64MB files) → Spark on EMR ETL to curated Parquet partitioned by `dt/hour/event_type` → Iceberg tables for ACID and schema enforcement → Trino for ad-hoc SQL → Spark ML for feature engineering. Storage: S3 Standard for first 30 days (~$0.023/GB-month), lifecycle to S3 IA after 30 days ($0.0125), Glacier after 90 days ($0.004). At ~500 bytes/event * 5B events/day = 2.5 TB/day raw, ~75 TB/month hot, ~$1.7K/month hot storage. Partition by `dt` and `event_type` (view, click, purchase) so queries on a specific event type scan only that subset. Use Iceberg hidden partitioning on `event_timestamp` so analysts query by timestamp without knowing the partition column. Schema: enforce at the curated zone via Iceberg schema, reject bad events to a dead-letter bucket. Catalog: AWS Glue with DataHub for discovery and OpenLineage for lineage. Access: Lake Formation column-level for PII (user_id, email masked). Compression: Parquet with Snappy (4–10x smaller than JSON). Compaction: run Iceberg compaction daily to merge small files into 256MB–1GB target. Cost: storage ~$2K/month hot, compute (EMR Spark + Trino) ~$50–100K/month, dominated by query compute.
**Visual:**
```
Kafka (60K/sec) -> Firehose (64MB, 1min) -> S3 raw/dt=.../event_type=...
Spark ETL -> Iceberg curated (Parquet, schema enforced, dt/hour partitions)
Trino -> ad-hoc SQL, Spark ML -> features
S3 lifecycle: Standard(30d) -> IA(90d) -> Glacier(1yr)
cost: storage $2K/mo, compute $50-100K/mo (queries dominate)
```

### Q2. Your data lake has 10 million small Parquet files in the curated zone, and Trino queries are slow. How do you fix it?
**Answer:** The small-files problem. Trino (and Spark, Hive) plans queries by listing files in S3, and 10M files means 10M S3 LIST+HEAD requests before any data is read — that listing alone can take minutes. Fixes in order of impact: (1) **Compact existing files** — run an Iceberg/Delta compaction job that reads small files and rewrites them into 256MB–1GB target files, reducing file count 10–100x. Iceberg's `rewrite_data_files` procedure does this in place with no downtime. (2) **Fix the ingestion pipeline** — the root cause is likely Firehose rotating at 1-minute intervals or Spark writing with too many partitions; increase rotation size (5-minute, 128MB) or coalesce Spark output. (3) **Tune metastore statistics** — run `ANALYZE TABLE` so the planner has accurate stats and can skip partitions. (4) **Use Iceberg manifests** — Iceberg stores file lists in Avro manifests, so planning does not require S3 LIST; this is the structural fix. (5) **Partition pruning** — ensure queries include partition filters (`WHERE dt = '2024-03-15'`) so only relevant partitions are scanned. (6) **Caching** — Trino's `cache.enabled=true` caches Parquet metadata and S3 file listings across queries. (7) **Alluxio or S3 Select pushdown** — for repeated queries, cache hot data locally. After compaction, 10M files should become ~100K files, and queries that took minutes drop to seconds. Ongoing: schedule weekly compaction jobs to prevent regression.
**Visual:**
```
problem: 10M small Parquet files -> Trino spends minutes on S3 LIST+HEAD
fix 1:   Iceberg rewrite_data_files (target 256MB-1GB) -> 100K files
fix 2:   fix ingest: Firehose 5min/128MB rotation, Spark coalesce
fix 3:   ANALYZE TABLE for stats, Iceberg manifests (no S3 LIST)
fix 4:   Trino cache.enabled=true, partition filters in queries
```

### Q3. You need to support GDPR "right to erasure" requests — delete all data for a specific user on request. How do you implement this in a data lake?
**Answer:** Erasure is hard in immutable data lakes because Parquet files are write-once; you cannot delete a single row without rewriting the file. Three approaches: (1) **Iceberg row-level DELETE** — Iceberg supports `DELETE FROM table WHERE user_id = ?` which marks the affected files as deleted in the metadata and rewrites only those files with the user's rows removed. This is the cleanest approach: the user's data is gone from the table, but the underlying Parquet files may still exist until compaction. Run compaction after the delete to physically remove the old files. (2) **Tokenization + key destruction** — tokenize `user_id` at ingestion, so all data references a token; for erasure, destroy the token-to-identity mapping in the vault, making the user's data unattributable without rewriting. This satisfies GDPR's "anonymization" without file rewrites. (3) **TTL + isolation** — partition by `user_id_hash` so each user's data is in a small set of files; on erasure, delete those specific partitions. For PII in free-text fields (chat transcripts), run NLP-based redaction. Operationally: build a self-service erasure API that takes a user ID, finds all tables containing that user (via the catalog), issues Iceberg DELETEs, runs compaction, and certifies completion. Track erasure requests in an audit log for compliance. Timeline: must complete within 30 days of request per GDPR. Cost: a typical erasure rewrites 1–10 GB across a few tables — negligible.
**Visual:**
```
option 1: Iceberg DELETE FROM table WHERE user_id=? -> rewrite affected files
option 2: tokenize at ingest, destroy token-to-identity mapping on erasure
option 3: partition by user_id_hash, delete specific partitions
ops:     self-service API -> find tables -> DELETE -> compact -> certify
SLA:     GDPR 30 days, audit log for compliance
```

### Q4. Your data scientists complain that they cannot find datasets in the lake, and 5 different "revenue" tables exist with conflicting numbers. How do you fix this?
**Answer:** This is the data swamp symptom. The fix is governance, not storage. Steps: (1) **Implement a catalog** — deploy DataHub or Amundsen, crawl all S3 datasets and metastore tables, and expose a search UI. Each dataset page shows schema, owner, freshness, sample data, and lineage. (2) **Identify the 5 revenue tables** — query the catalog for tables named `*revenue*`, trace each one's lineage to its source, and determine which is authoritative. Likely candidates: one built by the billing team from order records, one built by analytics from clickstream purchases, one built by finance from a different source. The "true" revenue is the one from the billing system; the others are derivatives with different definitions (gross vs net, US-only vs global, etc.). (3) **Deprecate duplicates** — mark the non-authoritative tables as `deprecated=true` in the catalog, redirect consumers to the authoritative one, and schedule a deletion after a 90-day grace period. (4) **Document the definition** — add a description: "Revenue = sum of completed order amounts, net of refunds, excluding taxes, USD." (5) **Enforce ownership** — every table must have an owning team and an on-call rotation; pipelines that write to the table are owned by that team. (6) **Add quality tests** — dbt tests or Great Expectations that fail the pipeline if revenue is null, negative, or outside expected range. (7) **Set up metric layer** — tools like dbt Metrics or Cube define canonical metrics once, with one SQL definition, so future "revenue" questions have one answer.
**Visual:**
```
problem: 5 revenue tables, conflicting numbers, no owner
fix:  catalog (DataHub) -> find all revenue tables -> trace lineage
      identify authoritative (billing system source) -> deprecate others
      document definition -> assign owner -> add quality tests
      metric layer (dbt Metrics) -> one canonical 'revenue' definition
```

### Q5. You need to ingest 50 PostgreSQL databases' CDC streams into the data lake. How do you design the pipeline?
**Answer:** Architecture: Debezium connectors on each Postgres (50 instances) → Kafka (one topic per table, ~500 topics) → Kafka Connect S3 sink writing Avro to `s3://lake/raw/<db>/<table>/dt=.../` → Spark ETL to Iceberg curated tables with upserts → Trino for query. Key design decisions: (1) **Format**: Avro with Schema Registry — Postgres schemas evolve, and Avro's schema evolution handles added columns gracefully. (2) **Partitioning**: partition by `dt` and `db_name`, not by primary key (would create millions of partitions). (3) **Upserts**: use Iceberg MERGE INTO to apply CDC records to the curated table — primary-key-based upsert keeps the curated table in sync with Postgres. (4) **Schema evolution**: when Postgres adds a column, the Avro schema registers a new version, and Iceberg's schema evolution propagates the column to the curated table without rewriting historical data. (5) **Backfill**: initial snapshot each Postgres table (could be TB) via Debezium's snapshot mode, writing directly to S3 in 1GB Parquet files. (6) **Monitoring**: track lag per topic (Debezium metrics in Datadog), alert if lag > 1 hour. (7) **Cost**: 50 databases * ~10 GB/day change volume = 500 GB/day raw, ~$0.023/GB-month = ~$350/month hot storage. Compute (Spark merge jobs) is the dominant cost — run merges every hour to keep curated fresh. (8) **Data quality**: validate CDC records have non-null primary keys, alert on schema changes. Avoid: writing JSON instead of Avro (no schema evolution), partitioning by primary key, running merges too frequently (small files).
**Visual:**
```
50 Postgres -> Debezium -> Kafka (500 topics, Avro+Schema Registry)
  -> Kafka Connect S3 sink -> s3://lake/raw/<db>/<table>/dt=.../
Spark ETL: Iceberg MERGE INTO curated USING raw ON primary_key
  -> curated tables stay in sync with Postgres (CDC applied hourly)
monitor: Debezium lag per topic, alert if >1h; schema evolution handled
```

### Q6. Your lake's storage cost is $80K/month for 3PB of mostly-cold data. How do you cut it?
**Answer:** Three levers: lifecycle tiering, compression, and deduplication. (1) **Lifecycle tiering** — audit which data is hot vs cold; if 80% of queries hit data from the last 30 days, age everything older to S3 IA ($0.0125/GB-month, half of Standard), older than 90 days to S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval ($0.004), older than 1 year to Glacier Deep Archive ($0.00099). For 3PB: if 100TB hot, 500TB IA, 1PB Glacier IR, 1.4PB Glacier DA, monthly cost = $2.3K + $6.3K + $4.1K + $1.4K = $14K/month, down from $69K/month for all-Standard. (2) **Compression** — ensure all Parquet files use Snappy or ZSTD compression (ZSTD gives 1.5–2x over Snappy at small CPU cost); many lakes have uncompressed JSON or CSV that could be 5–10x smaller as compressed Parquet. (3) **Deduplication** — identify duplicate datasets (same data ingested by multiple teams) via the catalog's column-fingerprint feature; consolidate to one canonical copy. (4) **Delete obsolete data** — many lakes hold years of data nobody queries; audit access logs (S3 server access logs or CloudTrail) and identify datasets with zero reads in 12 months; archive or delete them. (5) **Compaction** — small files cost more to query but not more to store; still, compacting 10M small files into 100K large files reduces metadata and query cost. (6) **Reserved capacity or Savings Plans** — for the compute side (EMR, Trino), commit to 1- or 3-year savings plans for 30–70% discounts. Combined, these can cut a $80K/month bill to $20–30K/month without losing any data.
**Visual:**
```
lifecycle: Standard(30d) -> IA(90d) -> Glacier IR(1yr) -> Glacier DA(>1yr)
3PB: 100TB hot + 500TB IA + 1PB IR + 1.4PB DA = ~$14K/mo (was $69K all-Standard)
compression: ZSTD on Parquet, 1.5-2x over Snappy
dedupe: catalog fingerprint -> consolidate duplicates
delete: audit S3 access logs, archive zero-read datasets
```

### Q7. Your ML team wants to train a recommendation model on the lake's clickstream data, but training reads are slow. How do you optimize?
**Answer:** The bottleneck is likely the read path: Spark training jobs reading Parquet from S3 suffer from S3's 20–50ms latency per object GET, especially for many small files or random access patterns. Fixes: (1) **Feature store** — precompute ML features (user embeddings, item embeddings, interaction counts) into a dedicated feature store table, partitioned by `user_id_hash` for fast lookup, so training reads pre-computed features instead of raw clicks. Tools: Feast, Tecton, or a simple Iceberg table. (2) **File format** — ensure features are in Parquet with row groups sized 128–256MB (one row group per S3 GET); avoid tiny row groups that require many requests. (3) **Caching** — deploy Alluxio or use Spark's built-in cache to keep hot datasets on local NVMe; for repeated training epochs, the second epoch reads from cache at memory speed. (4) **Co-locate compute and data** — run Spark on EC2 instances with local NVMe (i3, i4 instances) and prefetch the dataset to local disk at job start, so training reads from local NVMe at GB/s, not S3 at MB/s. (5) **Partition by user** — for models that read all of a user's history, partition by `user_id_hash` so all of one user's data is in one file, minimizing S3 requests. (6) **Vectorized reads** — use Parquet column pruning (read only needed columns) and predicate pushdown (skip row groups that don't match). (7) **Sampling** — for hyperparameter tuning, train on a 10% sample first, full data only for final training. (8) **Stream training** — for online learning, consume from Kafka directly instead of reading S3. Combined, these can take training time from hours to minutes.
**Visual:**
```
problem: Spark reads Parquet from S3, 20-50ms/object, many small files
fix 1: feature store (Feast) -> precomputed features, partitioned by user
fix 2: Parquet row groups 128-256MB (one S3 GET per row group)
fix 3: Alluxio or Spark cache for repeated epochs (memory speed)
fix 4: EC2 i3/i4 with local NVMe, prefetch dataset at job start
fix 5: partition by user_id_hash, column pruning, predicate pushdown
```
